strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in an original spectral analysis of latent diffusion models (Figure 1), extending prior pixel-space spectral autoregression observations (Dieleman, Rissanen et al.) to modern VAE latent spaces (SDXL, SD3.5) and directly justifying the core idea of scale-wise sampling.

Simple, practically elegant integration into an existing SOTA distillation framework (DMD2) that requires no additional trainable parameters or routers, in contrast to prior dynamic-inference methods.

Strong empirical validation across two model scales (SD3.5 Medium and Large), with both automated metrics (FID, CLIP score, ImageReward, PickScore, GenEval) and a large-scale human preference study conducted by professional assessors across four criteria (relevance, aesthetics, complexity, defects).

Substantial speedups (2.5x-10x) reported against strong, diverse baselines including diffusion distillation methods (DMD2-SDXL, SDXL-Turbo) and next-scale autoregressive models (Switti, Infinity), with SWD competitive or superior on most metrics.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual design choices: time-schedule shifting, scale schedule shape, scale-wise vs. full-scale training, synthetic vs. real training data, and PDM loss/kernel variants — these are repeated on two prompt sets (MJHQ, COCO) for robustness.

Novel Patch Distribution Matching (PDM) loss is simple (no extra trained models), motivated well via patch/token-level alignment on teacher features, and shown to be effective both as an auxiliary loss and as a standalone distillation objective.

Useful practical findings on implementation details (e.g., upscale-then-noise outperforms noise-then-upscale; pixel-space downscaling before VAE encoding outperforms latent-space downscaling) that are validated with controlled experiments (Table 1) and are likely useful to practitioners.

Interesting finding that SWD can correct pathological low-resolution generation failures of the teacher model itself (e.g., SDXL producing implausible images at 256x256, Figure 4), suggesting the method has value beyond pure speed-up.
weaknesses: The paper's headline claim of general superiority is undercut by mixed automated-metric results: e.g., Table 2 shows SWD has worse FID than full-scale at matched step counts (23.0 vs 20.4 at 6 steps, COCO), and the paper leans heavily on human evaluation to argue overall superiority without fully explaining or reconciling the FID gap.

SWD is only empirically integrated with one distillation backbone (DMD2); compatibility with adversarial distillation methods like ADD is asserted but never empirically demonstrated, weakening the generality claim.

The scale schedule (e.g., 256->384->512->640->768->1024) appears to be manually/heuristically chosen rather than derived from a principled criterion tied to the spectral analysis in Section 3; no systematic search or adaptive scheduling is explored, despite this being flagged as important future work.

Comparison baselines for the main SOTA table are somewhat narrow (DMD2-SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, Switti, Infinity); other prominent fast few-step distillation methods (e.g., LCM, Hyper-SD, SDXL-Lightning, consistency models) are not included, limiting the completeness of the positioning.

Human evaluation, while thorough, is the primary evidentiary basis for several core claims (e.g., quality improvement under matched compute budget), and the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement or statistical significance for the SbS results.

The mechanism behind why scale-wise training improves IR/PS while degrading FID is not deeply analyzed; a discussion of potential distribution-shift effects introduced by low-resolution/upscaled intermediate predictions would strengthen the technical understanding.

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations of the scale-wise approach (e.g., under very few steps, extreme scale ratios, or non-DiT architectures), which would help calibrate the scope of applicability.

strengths: The spectral analysis motivation (Section 3) linking noise levels to suppressed high-frequency content in VAE latents is a clear, interpretable justification for the core idea, extending prior spectral-autoregression observations to modern latent diffusion models (SDXL, SD3.5).
The proposed scale-wise sampling procedure is simple to implement on top of an existing distillation pipeline (DMD2) and requires no additional trainable modules or architecture changes.

The patch distribution matching (PDM) loss is a lightweight addition that reuses intermediate teacher features rather than training a separate discriminator/model, and the ablations show it also functions as a standalone objective.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (time-shift, scale schedule, scale-wise vs. full-scale training, real vs synthetic data, PDM kernel choice) support several individual design decisions.
Human preference studies with a described professional-assessor protocol complement automated metrics, and qualitative examples are provided for multiple prompts/models.
The method is validated on two model scales (SD3.5 Medium and Large), and reported latency reductions relative to full-scale counterparts and several open-source baselines are substantial.
weaknesses: FID is consistently worse than several baselines (e.g., SDXL, DMD2-SDXL) in Table 4 despite advantages in PickScore/ImageReward/GenEval; this inconsistency across metrics is not carefully analyzed or explained, raising concerns about what the improvements actually reflect (e.g., possible reward-model gaming via IR/PS rather than genuine fidelity gains).
The method is only integrated with a single distillation backbone (DMD2); the claimed compatibility with ADD/LADD-style methods is asserted but never empirically demonstrated.

Time and scale schedules appear to be manually hand-tuned (specific fixed lists of timesteps/resolutions) rather than learned or systematically optimized, and the paper itself flags adaptive scheduling as future work — the current approach's sensitivity to schedule choice is not fully explored beyond one or two configurations.

Evaluation is restricted to two closely related teacher models (SD3.5 Medium/Large); no experiments on UNet-based SDXL-style backbones or other architectures for the full method (only the failed-generation illustration in Fig. 4 touches SDXL), limiting evidence of generality despite claims about broad applicability to DiT models.

No code, pretrained weights, or explicit reproducibility statement is provided, which is a concern given the many implementation-specific details (LoRA ranks, guidance scales, schedules) needed to reproduce results.

Latency comparisons across very different architectures/parameter counts (e.g., Switti, Infinity, SDXL-based methods) may not be fully apples-to-apples, and the paper does not discuss confidence intervals or variance in the human evaluation results shown only as point estimates with sparse error bars.

The core idea largely combines two well-established prior directions (next-scale/coarse-to-fine generation and distribution-matching distillation) with an incremental new loss (PDM); the technical novelty beyond this combination is relatively limited.
Ablations for the full pipeline (Table 5/7) are conducted only on SD3.5 Medium at a single step count (6 steps), leaving open whether conclusions hold for SD3.5 Large or other step budgets.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea connecting next-scale prediction with diffusion distillation, grounded in a clear spectral analysis (Fig. 1) showing that high frequencies are masked by noise at high noise levels, providing intuitive justification for scale-wise sampling.

Careful empirical validation of key design choices, e.g., the upsampling ordering experiment (Table 1) showing that upscaling clean predictions before noise injection is far better than the alternatives, and the importance of time-schedule shifting.

The proposed Patch Distribution Matching (PDM) loss is simple, requires no additional trainable models, integrates easily into existing distillation pipelines, and is shown to be effective both as an auxiliary loss and as a standalone distillation objective.

Comprehensive evaluation across two base models (SD3.5 Medium/Large), automated metrics (FID, CLIP, ImageReward, PickScore, GenEval), and professional human preference studies across four criteria (relevance, aesthetics, complexity, defects).

Strong efficiency gains: SWD approaches ~2x speedup over full-scale distillation at equal step counts and is reported to be 2.5x-10x faster than several state-of-the-art baselines while matching or exceeding their quality on most metrics.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 5, Table 7) isolating the contribution of time-shifting, scale schedule, scale-wise training vs. full-scale training, synthetic vs. real data, and PDM kernel choice.

Interesting side finding that scale-wise distillation can correct poor low-resolution generation behavior of the teacher model (e.g., SDXL producing garbage at 256x256), showing practical robustness of the method.
weaknesses: FID results are frequently worse for SWD than for full-scale or baseline models (e.g., Table 2 and Table 4 show SWD often has notably higher/worse FID than SDXL, DMD2-SDXL, and even full-scale configurations), which is only partially explained and could indicate distributional shift not fully captured by other metrics.

The scale and time schedules used in experiments (e.g., [256,384,512,640,768,1024]) appear largely hand-crafted with limited principled derivation or systematic search; only a few schedule variants are ablated (constant scale, time-shift on/off), leaving open how sensitive results are to schedule choice or how to select an optimal one in general.

Evaluation is limited to two related DiT-based backbones (SD3.5 Medium/Large); no experiments on UNet-based large-scale models (e.g., SDXL as a teacher/student directly, despite DMD2 originally targeting SDXL) or other architectures, limiting evidence of general applicability.

Training relies heavily on teacher-generated synthetic data, and using real data significantly hurts performance (Table 5, config D); this dependency on teacher self-consistency is a notable practical limitation not deeply analyzed.

Baseline comparisons in Table 4 mix models of substantially different sizes and training recipes (e.g., 2B vs 8B parameter models, adversarial training on external data for ADD/LADD variants) which somewhat complicates fair, apples-to-apples comparison despite the latency/parameter columns provided.

The extension to video generation and adaptive/dynamic scheduling are only mentioned as future work without any preliminary experiments, so the generality of the approach beyond static image generation remains unverified.

Additional training overhead and complexity introduced by maintaining a fake DM and discriminator (inherited from DMD2) is not clearly quantified relative to the reported speed benefits, and the added PDM loss's overhead (though claimed minimal) is not explicitly benchmarked in isolation.

strengths: Extends the spectral-autoregression view of diffusion to VAE latent spaces (image and, novelly, temporal dimension for video), providing empirical motivation for progressive/scale-wise generation directly in latent space.

Proposes SwD, a clean way to unify progressive multi-scale generation with existing distribution-matching distillation objectives (DMD/GAN) into a single few-step model, avoiding the need for separate cascaded models.

Introduces a simple patch-level MMD distillation loss in feature space that is shown to be a competitive standalone distillation objective and complements DMD/GAN losses, with informative ablations (kernel choice, per-image vs batch averaging, noised vs clean features).

Broad and careful empirical evaluation across four T2I backbones (SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, FLUX) and a T2V backbone (Wan2.1), using multiple automatic metrics (PS, HPSv3, IR, FID, GenEval, VBench2.0, VideoReward) plus a well-documented human preference study with clear annotation protocols.

Useful diagnostic experiments, e.g., showing that DMD-style distillation degrades when the teacher cannot generate plausible low-resolution samples while GAN/MMD losses are robust, and comparisons of noisy-latent upsampling strategies that justify the chosen design.

Reports consistent, practically meaningful speedups (~2x for T2I, ~3x for T2V) at matched step counts or against similarly fast baselines, supported by both automatic metrics and human studies, with reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (schedules, training/runtime setup).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: progressive/multi-scale generation (cascaded diffusion, Matryoshka diffusion, relay diffusion, f-DM, next-scale prediction models) is well established; the core contribution is largely an engineering combination of this idea with existing DMD/GAN distillation losses rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Timestep and scale schedules remain hand-tuned hyperparameters without a principled or automatic selection procedure, which limits generalizability to new architectures/resolutions and adds practical tuning burden.

Training relies exclusively on teacher-generated synthetic data with relatively short training (~3K iterations); while this is stated to avoid external-data bias, it complicates fair comparison with baselines (e.g., publicly released checkpoints such as DMD2, SDXL-Turbo, Hyper-SD) that were trained with different data/protocols by their original authors.

Mixed quality outcomes are reported in places (e.g., FLUX-SwD shows increased defects relative to Hyper-FLUX/FLUX; FID is noted to correlate poorly with human perception yet is still used as a primary metric), suggesting the improvements are not uniformly dominant across all quality axes.

The MMD objective, after simplification to a linear kernel, reduces to per-image patch-mean feature matching, which is conceptually close to feature-matching losses from GAN literature (as the paper itself acknowledges), somewhat limiting the technical novelty of this component in isolation.

Video evaluation is limited to a single teacher (Wan2.1-1.3B) and a single distilled baseline (CausVid), providing less breadth of comparison than the image experiments and leaving open how well the approach generalizes to other video backbones or larger-scale video models.

strengths: The spectral analysis extending the 'diffusion as spectral autoregression' idea to VAE latent spaces (both spatial and temporal dimensions for video) is a useful and reasonably rigorous empirical contribution that motivates the method well.

The scale-wise distillation (SwD) framework is practical and model-agnostic: it is demonstrated across five different base models (SDXL, SD3.5-M, SD3.5-L, FLUX, Wan2.1), spanning both text-to-image and text-to-video generation, which is a broad and convincing evaluation scope.

The proposed patch-level MMD loss is simple, requires no extra trainable discriminator, is computationally cheap (>7x faster iterations when used alone), and is shown to be a competitive standalone distillation objective as well as a useful addition to DMD/GAN losses.

The experimental evaluation is thorough: automatic metrics (FID, HPSv3, ImageReward, PickScore, GenEval, VBench2.0, VideoReward), professional human preference studies with well-documented evaluation protocols (Appendix H), and numerous ablations (upsampling strategy, kernel choice, batch vs per-image averaging, constant vs progressive scale schedules).

Good engineering details and transparency about limitations, e.g., explicit discussion of cases where the DMD loss fails (SDXL, Wan2.1) and why, and analysis of noisy-latent upsampling strategies (Appendix F).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the paper combines pre-existing ideas (progressive/cascaded multi-resolution diffusion, distribution matching distillation, GAN feature-matching losses) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the MMD loss is explicitly described as an adaptation of existing feature-matching losses to a pretrained-DM feature space.

The scale and timestep schedules remain hand-tuned hyperparameters without a principled, automated procedure for selecting them; the spectral analysis only provides average guidance and the paper admits the schedules 'ultimately remain hyperparameters,' which weakens the claimed link between the spectral analysis and the method's design.

The DMD component of the framework is shown to fail or degrade performance for SDXL and Wan2.1 due to teacher limitations at low resolution, requiring ad hoc exclusion of this loss for those models — this undercuts the claim that SwD 'integrates seamlessly' with existing distillation approaches.

No comparison against dedicated cascaded/progressive-resolution baselines (e.g., Matryoshka Diffusion, f-DM, relay diffusion) is provided despite these being discussed at length in related work; the only direct baselines are full-resolution few-step models, which is a narrower comparison than ideal.

Human evaluation shows SwD is not uniformly better: for FLUX, SwD exhibits noticeably more defects and lower text relevance than Hyper-FLUX/FLUX, and SDXL-SwD has more defects than SDXL-DMD2, suggesting the efficiency gains come with non-trivial, model-dependent quality trade-offs that are somewhat downplayed in the abstract/conclusion.

Reproducibility is only moderate: no public code/checkpoints are mentioned (only a project page placeholder), and several implementation choices (LoRA ranks, guidance scales, schedules) are scattered across appendices without a consolidated reproducible pipeline description.
FID is reported despite being explicitly acknowledged as poorly correlated with human perception for this task, raising questions about why it is still used as a primary metric in several tables.

strengths: The paper identifies an underexplored axis for diffusion distillation efficiency (spatial/temporal resolution) complementary to the well-studied step-count axis, and provides a clear spectral analysis (RAPSD) motivating that latent DMs can operate at lower resolution at high noise levels, extending prior pixel-space spectral autoregression findings to VAE latent spaces and to the temporal dimension of video diffusion.

The proposed SwD framework is simple, model-agnostic, and integrates cleanly with existing distribution-matching distillation approaches (DMD, ADD/GAN), requiring no architectural changes and working across multiple SOTA backbones (SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, FLUX, Wan2.1), which is a strong demonstration of generality.

The scale-transition strategy (renoising a predicted x0 rather than naively upsampling noisy latents) is a well-motivated design choice, supported by a controlled ablation (Table 1 and Appendix F) showing it better preserves the correct noise statistics.

The new MMD-based patch-level distillation loss (L_MMD) is simple, cheap (no auxiliary trainable network), and shown to be a competitive standalone distillation baseline as well as a helpful additional loss term, which is a useful contribution beyond the scale-wise framework itself.

Extensive experimental validation: automatic metrics (PS, HPSv3, IR, FID, GenEval, VBench-2.0, VisionReward, VideoReward) across 5 base models, professional human preference studies with detailed rubrics (relevance, defects, aesthetics, complexity), and multiple ablations (scale-wise vs full-resolution at matched steps and matched latency, MMD loss variants, constant vs progressive schedules, high-frequency detail preservation via patch FID/CLIP-IQA).

Reported efficiency gains are substantial and consistently demonstrated (~2x speedup for T2I, ~3x for T2V at equal steps, >10x over full-resolution teacher few-step baselines), with latency measured under a realistic, reproducible setup (FP16, torch.compile, TinyVAE, batch-normalized latency).

Good transparency about limitations, e.g., the explicit discussion that L_DMD degrades performance when the teacher cannot generate plausible low-resolution images (Appendix B), and appropriate ablation showing L_MMD-only training is more robust in that setting.
weaknesses: The scale/timestep schedules are described as hyperparameters chosen via limited, model-specific tuning; while the paper claims low sensitivity, only one schedule-comparison ablation (Table 9, constant vs progressive) is shown, and there is no systematic study of how much performance depends on schedule choice or how transferable schedules are across unseen architectures.

The favorable comparison of SwD against full-resolution counterparts at matched latency (rather than matched steps) partially conflates the benefits of the scale-wise idea with the specific choice of very few steps for the full-resolution baseline (e.g., 2 steps), which is known to be a particularly hard regime for full-resolution distillation; a more thorough Pareto-curve style comparison across a range of steps/latencies would strengthen the claims.

For SDXL and Wan2.1, the standard L_DMD component had to be dropped because it degrades performance when the teacher cannot generate low-resolution images well, and the paper relies solely on L_MMD/L_GAN for these models — this suggests the scale-wise framework's applicability with standard distribution-matching objectives is not fully general and depends on teacher characteristics not always known in advance without extra experimentation.

The video results rely on comparison to only one distilled baseline (CausVid, re-trained on the paper's own synthetic dataset rather than the original high-quality data), which limits how conclusive the T2V comparisons are; broader baseline coverage for video distillation would be useful.

The MMD loss ablation and most method-development experiments are conducted primarily on SD3.5-Medium, with limited comparable ablations shown for other backbones, so it's unclear how consistently the design choices (e.g., feature layer choice, kernel choice, timestep interval) generalize.

Human evaluation methodology, while detailed, is based on a relatively small prompt set (128 prompts) and only 3 raters per pair with majority voting, and inter-rater agreement / statistical significance are not reported, making it harder to assess the robustness of the human-preference conclusions.

The paper's core theoretical grounding (spectral autoregression argument) is empirical/averaged and admits notable exceptions (e.g., SDXL uses VP diffusion and shows different high-frequency behavior; latent regularization causes slightly noisy 'clean' latents), yet these nuances are not deeply integrated into the schedule design methodology, which remains largely heuristic.
